         AMERICAN STEWARDS OF LIBERTY’S BRIEFING ON REMANDED
                PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUE NOS. 11 AND 13

        COMES NOW, American Stewards of Liberty (ASL) and files it Briefing on Remanded

 Preliminary Order (PO) Issue Nos. 11 and 13, and in support thereof, shows as follows.

                                     I.       INTRODUCTION

        The Commission’s remand asks for additional answers, not additional evidence. The

 evidentiary record is closed, and Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission

 Services Corporation’s (collectively, the Applicants) burden remains unchanged. The question
 before the SOAH ALJs is a narrow one: whether the existing record supports different findings on

PO Issue Nos. 11 and 13 than those reflected in the Proposal for Decision (PFD). It does not.

        The distinction between clarifying the PFD and curing the evidentiary record is critical.

Applicants had the opportunity to establish that Import Path 2 is necessary to satisfy an identified

state or federal reliability standard and to quantify the congestion-cost savings to consumers

attributable to the proposed facilities. They did neither. Instead, Applicants presented Import

Path 2 as one component of a broader, integrated transmission plan designed to import power into

the Permian Basin. The PFD considered the evidence and concluded that Applicants failed to

establish the project-specific need for Import Path 2.

        The evidence identified by Applicants on remand (Applicants’ Directory 1) does not fill that

gap. As to PO Issue No. 11, evidence that ERCOT conducted system-wide planning pursuant to

NERC and ERCOT reliability criteria does not establish that Import Path 2 itself is necessary to

satisfy any identified reliability standard.         Applicants’ own witness acknowledged that the

individual lines were not studied independently, and the PFD found that no partial-build analysis

established the need for Import Path 2 separate and apart from the broader 765-kV plan. As to PO

Issue No. 13, the deficiency is even more straightforward: Applicants elected to proceed on a

reliability theory rather than an economic theory and never quantified the congestion-cost savings

attributable to Import Path 2. System-wide congestion figures and economic comparisons between

performed.

           The circumstances of the remand reinforce rather than diminish these deficiencies. The

PFDs in the other 765-kV proceedings addressed PO Issue Nos. 11 and 13 in substantially the

same manner, often noting simply that the parties did not focus on reliability or congestion-cost

savings. Those proceedings were not remanded for additional findings. What distinguishes this

proceeding is not the manner in which the PFD addressed those issues, but the result: here, the

SOAH ALJs concluded that the Applicants failed to establish need.

           The remand provides an opportunity to state the answers to PO Issue No. 11 and 13 more

expressly. It does not provide an opportunity to change the evidence necessary to support those

answers. On the closed evidentiary record before them, the SOAH ALJs should find that

Applicants did not establish that Import Path 2 is necessary to meet an identified state or federal

reliability standard, that the record contains no quantified estimate of congestion-cost savings to

consumers attributable to Import Path 2, and that neither issue provides a basis to disturb the PFD’s

determination that Applicants failed to establish need.

                                             II.    ARGUMENT

A.         The Commission’s remand applies a different standard to this PFD than it applied to
           the other 765-kV PFDs

           SOAH Order No. 35 directs the parties to brief PO Issue Nos. 11 and 13 following the

Commission’s remand of this proceeding. 2 The SOAH ALJs determined that the evidentiary

record will not be reopened. 3 Accordingly, the task on remand is limited: the SOAH ALJs must

ASL Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                              Page 3
 answer PO Issue Nos. 11 and 13 based on the evidence already admitted. The remand neither

supplements that evidence nor alters Applicants’ burden to establish the need for Import Path 2.

        The circumstances giving rise to the remand are nevertheless important. The Commission

purportedly remanded this proceeding because it concluded that the PFD did not sufficiently

address whether the proposed facilities are necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards

under PO Issue No. 11 or the estimated congestion-cost savings to consumers under PO Issue No.

13. 4 But the manner in which the PFD addressed those issues was not unique to this proceeding.

The PFDs in Docket Nos. 59029, 59315, and 59336 treated the same PO issues in substantially the

same manner—and, in some instances, with even less analysis—without prompting a remand.

        For example, in Docket No. 59029, the PFD introduced Issues 11 through 13 by stating

that “[t]he parties do not focus on reliability or congestion cost[] savings.” 5 As to PO Issue No.

11, the PFD included a footnote summarizing Oncor’s contention that ERCOT had observed

thermal and voltage criteria violations, voltage instability, and unsolved power flow and that the

project would increase reliability and address reliability issues associated with load growth. 6 The

PFD did not separately identify a particular state or federal reliability standard and determine that

the proposed facilities were necessary to satisfy it. Nor did the PFD quantify estimated congestion-

cost savings to consumers under PO Issue No. 13. 7

        The PFD in Docket No. 59336 employed essentially the same approach. After reciting PO

Issue Nos. 11 and 13, the SOAH ALJs stated simply that “[t]he parties do not focus on reliability

        Docket No. 59315 contained somewhat greater discussion, but its treatment of PO Issue

No. 13 is similarly instructive. The PFD states that “[t]he parties do not focus on cost congestion

savings” and then summarized testimony from Oncor witness Jared Gurley that the transmission

system between West Texas and other portions of the State experiences severe congestion, that the

PBRP import paths would relieve that congestion, and that congestion-cost savings “could be

significant based on ERCOT estimates.” 9

        The PFD in Docket No. 59475 therefore did not depart from the analytical approach taken

in the preceding 765-kV proceedings. It expressly identified PO Issue No. 11 and 13 and addressed

them in light of the theory of need Applicants chose to present. As to PO Issue No. 11, the SOAH

ALJs explained that Applicants presented Import Path 2 as a project that would import power from

elsewhere in Texas into the Permian Basin, “not that the proposed transmission facilities are

necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards.” 10 As to PO Issue No. 13, the SOAH ALJs

explained that Applicants characterized Import Path 2 as a reliability project and did not submit

the requested estimate of congestion-cost savings to consumers. 11 The SOAH ALJs further

recognized Applicants’ argument that reliability projects are exempt from the economic tests

 applicable to economic projects and concluded that a congestion-cost-savings analysis was

therefore not required.

           The material difference between Docket Nos. 59182 and 59475 and the other 765-kV

proceedings is therefore not that the 59475 PFD uniquely failed to discuss PO Issues No. 11

and 13. The material difference is the result of the need analysis. Here, unlike in the preceding

PFDs, the SOAH ALJs concluded that Applicants failed to establish need for the proposed project.

           That distinction makes the Commission’s stated basis for remand difficult to reconcile with

its treatment of the preceding 765-kV proceedings. If the PO required a separate affirmative

determination identifying the particular state or federal reliability standards necessitating each

project and a definition of those standards—as the Commission claims—then the same concern

should have existed in Docket Nos. 59029 and 59336. And, if PO Issue No. 13 required a

determination of the estimated congestion-cost savings to consumers notwithstanding Applicants’

reliance on a reliability theory of need, the same concern existed in Docket Nos. 59029, 59316,

and 59336. Yet those PFDs were not returned to SOAH for further findings on that basis.

B.         PO Issue No. 11: Applicants did not establish that Import Path 2 is necessary to meet
           an identified state or federal reliability standard

           PO Issue No. 11 asks whether “the proposed transmission facilities” are necessary to meet

state or federal reliability standards.” 12 Applicants now identify portions of the record discussing

NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1, ERCOT Protocols, ERCOT planning criteria, Generic

Transmission Constraints (GTCs), and ERCOT’s broader reliability planning. Those citations

establish that ERCOT considered reliability standards when conducting its system-wide planning

analyses. They do not resolve the question actually presented by PO Issue No. 11: whether these




12
     PO at 13 (Mar. 30, 2026).


ASL Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                               Page 6
 proposed transmission facilities—Import Path 2—are necessary to meet an identified state or

federal reliability standard.

        i.      Compliance with NERC planning standards is not the same as a finding that Import
                Path 2 is required by those standards.

        Applicants rely heavily on the PBRP’s statement that its “reliability assessments were

performed based on NERC Reliability Standard TLP-001-5.1, ERCOT Protocols, and ERCOT

Planning Criteria.” 13 The PBRP likewise states that its steady-state reliability analysis was

performed in accordance with TPL-001-5.1 and identified a need for substantial local and regional

transmission upgrades. 14       Applicants’ witness Mr. Gurley similarly testified that ERCOT

performed its reliability studies in accordance with TPL-001-5.1, the ERCOT Planning Guide, and

the ERCOT Nodal Protocols. 15

        But those citations establish the methodology governing ERCOT’s planning studies, not

that TPL-001-5.1 requires Import Path 2. That distinction is evident from Applicants’ own

evidence. The PBRP states broadly that “multiple import paths would be needed” after evaluating

projected generation and that ERCOT recommended significant transmission upgrades “based on

the study assumptions.” 16 It does not identify a particular TPL-001-5.1 violation that can be cured

only by Import Path 2, nor does it establish that the Bell County East-to-Big Hill and Big Hill-to-

Sand Lake facilities are independently necessary to maintain compliance with that standard.

        Applicants’ reliance on the 2024 and 2025 Regional Transmission Plans suffers from the

same problem. Those studies were conducted, in part, to satisfy ERCOT’s obligations under

NERC reliability standards and identified reliability needs across the ERCOT system. 17 But

 evidence that ERCOT conducted a system-wide planning study pursuant to NERC standard does

not establish that every transmission facility embedded in the resulting base case is itself

“necessary to meet” that standard.

        Indeed, Applicants’ own evidence demonstrates the distinction.             The 2025 RTP

incorporated the entire 765-kV STEP into its starting base cases and then found no more need to

remove any element. 18 A study that assumes the entire 765-kV STEP as part of its starting

topology does not independently establish that Import Path 2 is necessary. It assumes the very

infrastructure whose necessity is at issue.

        ii.      Applicants’ own evidence confirms that Import Path 2 was not independently
                 studied

        Most significantly, Applicants cite Mr. Gurley’s admission on cross examination: “I am

not aware of a study that isolated each line independently as they were—they were studied

together.” 19 That admission goes directly to the defect identified in the PFD.

        Applicants now ask the SOAH ALJs to infer project-specific necessity from studies that

Applicants’ own witness acknowledges did not isolate the individual facilities whose necessity the

Commission must determine.             Yet, the PFD already addressed that problem, finding that

Applicants “did not perform a partial build study to justify the need for Import Path 2 individually”

and “did not establish the need for Import Path 2 separate and apart from the three 765-kV import

paths as one comprehensive project.” 20 The SOAH ALJs further found that NERC contingencies

influencing ERCOT’s regional planning “are not a substitute for proving project-specific need for

18
   Applicants’ Ex. 17 (Gurley Rebuttal), Ex. JG-R-3 (2025 RTP) at 28.
19

ASL Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                              Page 8
 Import Path 2.” 21 Applicants identify no evidence undermining those findings. To the contrary,

Mr. Gurley’s testimony confirms them.

           That omission is particularly significant because ERCOT’s reliability analysis does not

establish that transmission was the only means of addressing the underlying reliability concern.

Transmission determines the capacity to move power between locations; it does not determine how

much generation will exist, where that generation will be located, or whether sufficient power will

be available to use that transmission capacity if called upon. A finding that the system requires

additional reliable capacity therefore does not, standing alone, establish that a particular long-

distance transmission line is necessary to provide that capacity.

           Nor did Applicants isolate those variables.                 They did not study Import Path 2

independently, did not perform a partial-build analysis, and did not establish that the reliability

condition they identify could be satisfied only through this Project rather than through a different

combination or location of generation and transmission resources. Without that analysis, the

record may explain why ERCOT selected Import Path 2 as part of its preferred system-wide

solution, but it does not establish that Import Path 2 itself is necessary to satisfy an identified

reliability standard.

           This distinction is particularly important because the Legislature did not incorporate a

comprehensive need determination for the PBRP projects in HB 5066. 22 Applicants must therefore

establish the necessity of the facilities for which they seek CCNs under PURA § 37.056. The fact

that ERCOT studied a portfolio of projects under NERC planning criteria does not establish that

every constituent project independently satisfies that burden.

ASL Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                                 Page 9
          iii.     The Far West GTC evidence does not cure the project-specific deficiency

         Applicants also rely heavily on the Far West Import GTCs, which ERCOT designated as

Interconnection Reliability Operating Limits (IROLs). Mr. Martin testified that exceeding those

limits could result in cascading thermal overloads and that ERCOT identified the three 765-kV

import paths, including Import Path 2, as components of its GTC exit strategy. 23 That evidence

merely demonstrates the existence of operational constraints in Far West Texas. It does nothing

to establish that Import Path 2 itself is necessary to resolve them.

         ERCOT’s GTC exit strategy identifies multiple projects. Applicants’ own evidence states

that ERCOT identified six transmission projects for the North-to-Far West GTC and eight for the

South-to-Far West GTC. 24 The fact that Import Path 2 appears among a portfolio of projects

expected to assist in retiring those constraints does not establish that the constraint cannot be

resolved without Import Path 2 or that particular Project is independently required by FAC-001-4

or any other NERC standard.

         Thus, the PFD expressly considered this evidence and correctly found that the Far West

Import GTCs did not establish the necessity of Import Path 2. The SOAH ALJs determined that

the GTCs measure transmission-system constraints but do not validate the composition or

reliability of the load driving the PBRP forecast; that Applicants did not disaggregate the load

driving the GTCs from the speculative load undermining that forecast; and that the GTC evidence

therefore does not validate either the original PBRP forecast or the necessity of Import Path 2. 25

         Nothing in Applicants’ Directory changes those findings.

ASL Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                            Page 10
            iv.      Applicants’ reliability evidence still depends on the same factual premise the PFD
                    rejected

           More fundamentally, Applicants’ PO Issue No. 11 evidence cannot be separated from the

deficiencies underlying the PFD’s need determination. Mr. Gurley testified that local upgrades

were insufficient because of “the amount of local load growth and the lack of adequate

conventional generation in the Permian Basin,” which led ERCOT to identify import paths

necessary to transfer power into the region. 26 The PBRP likewise states that multiple import paths

are needed to transfer power into the Permian Basin after evaluating projected generation. 27

           Those are the same factual premises the PFD found unreliable.

           Applicants’ theory necessarily assumes more than the existence of a transmission

constraint. If the asserted reliability function of Import Path 2 is to import power into the Permian

Basin during periods when local generation is insufficient, then the Project can perform that

function only if sufficient generation exists elsewhere in the system, is available at the relevant

time, and can reach the eastern terminus of Import Path 2 for delivery westward. Transmission

capacity cannot substitute for generation capacity. An import path creates the ability to move

power; it does not create the power to be moved.

           That distinction exposes the fundamental flaw with Applicants’ reliability showing. The

proposed solution effectively assumes that new generation will exist outside the Permian Basin

and be available for import when needed. But the location of future generation is itself a planning

assumption, not an established fact. Additional reliable generation located closer to the projected

load would necessarily change the amount of long-distance import capability required, just as

additional load or insufficient generation near the eastern end of the Project would change the



26
     Applicants’ Ex. 3 (Gurley Direct) at 20-21.
27
     Applicants’ Ex. 1 (Application), Att. 5 (PBRP) at 15-17.


ASL Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                              Page 11
 amount of power available for westward transfer. Yet Applicants did not test those possibilities

in determining whether this Project is necessary.

           The SOAH ALJs correctly identified that evidentiary gap. Applicants failed to establish

that sufficient power would be available at Bell County East to transmit westward over Import

Path 2; neither Applicants nor ERCOT analyzed Central Texas’s net generation position under

current conditions, projected 2030 conditions, or projected conditions incorporating substantial

queued large loads; Applicants did not determine whether Central Texas generation could

simultaneously serve local data-center demand and export westward; and no sensitivity analysis

evaluated the viability of Import Path 2 if Central Texas generation proved insufficient to perform

both functions. 28 The PFD therefore correctly concluded that “the record does not establish that

Import Path 2 is needed for reliability.” 29

           That finding is especially significant because the Project’s asserted reliability function

depends upon the very fact Applicants failed to establish. The question is not simply whether

additional transmission capacity would permit more power to flow westward. Of course it would.

The question is whether sufficient power will actually exist at the eastern end of the Project to

make that additional transfer capability a reliable solution to the identified problem.

           Applicants’ Directory does not identify any record evidence that filled this evidentiary gap.

The Directory simply collects the same planning studies and testimony the SOAH ALJs already

considered in reaching their determination.

           Nor does the evidence regarding the Far West Import GTCs eliminate that problem. Those

constraints arise precisely because Far West Texas requires imports during periods of insufficient

local generation. Building another path labeled as an “import path” does not establish that


28
     PFD at 86-88; PFD at 189-90, FOF Nos. 121-26.
29
     Id. at 190, FOF No. 127.


ASL Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                                Page 12
 sufficient power exists at its eastern source to make the path capable of performing that function.

As the PFD recognized, the reliability of the asserted solution depends upon both transmission

capacity and power available to be transmitted.

        The timing of the asserted solution reinforces the point. The premise of the PBRP is

substantial load growth requiring additional reliable capacity.          But meeting additional load

necessarily requires additional generation somewhere on the ERCOT system regardless of whether

Import Path 2 is constructed. The transmission line determines where that generation may be

located and how it may reach load, but it does not eliminate the need for the generation itself.

Thus, before a particular import path can be deemed “necessary” for reliability, the analysis must

establish not merely a need for additional power in the importing region, but why that power must

be supplied through this transmission path rather than through a different combination of

generation location, local upgrades, and transmission resources.

        Applicants did not make that showing. Instead, the analysis moves from projected load

growth and insufficient local generation to the conclusion that long-distance imports are necessary,

while treating the future availability and location of the generation supplying those imports as an

assumption. That reasoning risks turning a planning choice into a reliability necessity: once the

model assumes where generation will and will not be located, transmission necessary to

accommodate that assumed generation pattern can appear indispensable. But that does not

establish that the transmission facility itself is required by a state or federal reliability standard.

        This is particularly problematic here because Applicants seek to use PO Issue No. 11 as an

independent basis for finding necessity after the PFD rejected the underlying need showing. The

same unsupported factual premise cannot do different work merely because it is not characterized

as “reliability.”   Whether considered under the broader need inquiry or PO Issue No. 11




ASL Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                                 Page 13
 specifically, the asserted reliability function of Import Path 2 still depends upon sufficient power

being available for the Project to transmit.

           Applicants therefore cannot bridge the evidentiary gap by pointing to NERC standards,

GTCs, or ERCOT planning criteria. Those authorities may establish the reliability conditions

ERCOT must plan for. They do not establish that Import Path 2 is the necessary means of

satisfying them. And they certainly do not supply the missing evidence concerning whether

sufficient generation will be available at Bell County East to permit Import Path 2 to perform the

westward-import function on which Applicants’ reliability theory depends.

           Accordingly, Applicants’ citations establish that ERCOT employed NERC and ERCOT

reliability criteria in developing the PBRP and broader 765-kV plan. They do not establish the

proposition posed by PO Issue No. 11: that Import Path 2 itself is necessary to meet an identified

state or federal reliability standard. The supplemental PFD should answer PO Issue No. 11

accordingly.

C.         PO Issue No. 13: The record contains no estimate of congestion-cost savings to
           consumers

           Applicants’ Directory similarly identifies evidence concerning congestion. But here again,

Applicants attempt to answer a project-specific question with system-wide evidence. PO Issue

No. 13 does not ask whether congestion exists in ERCOT, whether 765-kV transmission generally

can alleviate congestion, or whether the entire 765-kV STEP performs better economically than

an alternative. It asks for “estimated congestion cost savings for consumers that may result from

the proposed transmission facilities.” 30 Applicants identify no analysis estimating the congestion-

cost savings attributable to Import Path 2.




30
     PO at 13 (Mar. 30, 2026).


ASL Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                             Page 14
         i.       The numerical estimates Applicants identify compare entire transmission plans, not
                 Import Path 2

        Applicants seemingly rely most heavily on ERCOT’s comparison of the 765-kV STEP

against the alternative 345-kV plan. That analysis found that the entire 765-kV plan would have

approximately $94 million less congestion rent than the 345-kV plan in 2034 and approximately

$172 million less congestion rent in 2039. 31 It also estimated that, in the long term, the 765-kV

STEP would produce approximately $229 million more annual consumer-energy-cost savings than

the 345-kV plan. 32 Those figures do not answer PO Issue No. 13.

        The comparison is 765-kV plan versus 345-kV plan. It does not compare ERCOT system

congestion with and without Import Path 2. Nor does it isolate the Bell County East-to-Big Hill

and Big Hill-to-Sand Lake facilities from the remainder of the 765-kV STEP. Accordingly, the

$94 million, $172 million, and $229 million figures cannot be attributed to Import Path 2.

        The distinction is apparent from the tables themselves. The economic study reports results

for the “2034 Base Case,” “2034 345-kV Plan,” and “2034 765-kV Plan,” and repeats the same

plan-level comparison for 2039. 33 There is no “765-kV Plan Without Import Path 2” scenario

against which the incremental congestion benefit of these proposed facilities can be measured.

        That omission mirrors the problem with Applicants’ PO Issue No. 11 evidence: ERCOT

studied the facilities together rather than isolating Import Path 2. Applicants cannot take an

economic benefit attributed to the entire 765-kV portfolio and assign that benefit to one component

without evidence establishing that allocation.

   Applicants’ Ex. 3 (Gurley Direct), Ex. JG-4 (2024 RTP and Texas 765-kV Strategic Transmission Expansion Plan
Comparison) at 18-19.
32
   Id. at iv.

ASL Briefing on Remanded Preliminary Order Issues                                                      Page 15
          ii.       Applicants conflate congestion rent, production-cost savings, and consumer-
                   energy-cost savings

         Applicants’ Directory also places several distinct economic concepts together under PO

Issue No. 13. But the cited ERCOT tables distinguish among “Production Cost,” “Consumer

Energy Cost,” and “Congestion Rent.” 34 Those are separate metrics.

         For 2034, for example, the table reports that the 765-kV plan has $94 million less

congestion rent than the 345-kV plan, while its reported consumer-energy cost is actually

$136 million higher than the 345-kV plan. 35 For 2039, the 765-kV plan has $172 million less

congestion rent and $229 million lower consumer-energy cost than the 345-kV plan. 36

         That distinction matters because PO Issue No. 13 specifically asks for the estimated

“congestion cost savings for consumers.” Applicants cannot simply aggregate references to

production-cost savings, congestion rent, and consumer-energy costs and characterize them all as

the requested consumer congestion-cost savings. At minimum, the evidence must establish what

metric answers the PO question and how that benefit is attributable to the proposed facilities.

Applicants’ Directory does neither.

         Indeed, the 2034 results illustrate why that analytical step cannot simply be assumed.

Although the 765-kV plan produces lower congestion rent than the 345-kV alternative, the table

reports high consumer-energy cost for the 765-kV plan in that year. 37 Thus, even at the system-

wide plan level, reduced congestion rent does not necessarily translate directly into lower

consumer-energy costs.
